title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: GAR 2 — non mirum; temporal deferral
pass_a_gloss: GAR. 2. There is nothing wonderful in this, that Adam both at once from the sin incurred the privation of righteousness, and was not damned with eternal death, nor at once felt temporal death. Into spiritual death he at once ran, God so willing, lest if at once no species of death had run upon him, Satan's promise, you will not die at all, might seem to Adam truer than God's threat, by death you will die; and Adam growing old in sin might perhaps not have thought of serious repentance and conversion to God: but the sense of present punishment pricked him, that by repenting he might return to God, whom by rebelling he had deserted. But temporal death he did not at once incur, that time of repenting might be granted him, which is none after death. This punishment Adam would have paid on the same day on which he sinned, unless it had seemed good to God, on account of the future Satisfaction of Christ, to give space to the human race for doing repentance, says the Learned Man, Disputation on the fall of Adam, last Thesis. Finally eternal death he did not incur at all, because he was among the elect of God, over whom hell has no right. Apocalypse.
pass_b_english: Garissoles. 2. No wonder Adam at once lost righteousness by the sin, and yet was not damned to eternal death, nor felt bodily death at once. He fell into spiritual death at once—God willing it—lest, if no kind of death had struck him at once, Satan's promise (you will not die at all) should look truer to Adam than God's threat (you will die the death); and lest Adam, growing old in sin, should never think of serious repentance and return to God. The sting of present punishment pricked him so that he might repent and come back to the God he had left by rebellion.

Bodily death he did not meet at once, so that time to repent might be given him—there is none after death. He would have paid that penalty the very day he sinned, had God not, for Christ's coming Satisfaction, chosen to give the human race space for repentance (so the Learned Man says in his Disputation on Adam's fall, last thesis). Eternal death he never met at all, because he was among God's elect, over whom hell has no claim. (Apocalypse.)
source_text: GAR. 2. Nihil in eo mirum quod Adamus & statim a peccato privationem justitiae incurrit, & nec aeterna morte damnatus est, nec temporalem statim sensit. In spiritualem statim incurrit, ita volente Deo, ne si statim in eum non incurrisset ulla species mortis, videri posset Adamo verior Satanae promissio, non moriemini omnino, quam Dei comminatio, morte moriemini; & in peccato consenescens Adamus de seria poenitentia & conversione ad Deum forte non cogitasset: sed pupugit eum praesentis poenae sensus, ut ad Deum resipiscendo rediret, quem rebellando deseruerat. Mortem vero temporalem non statim incurrit, ut poenitendi tempus ipsi concederetur, quod nullum est post mortem. Hanc poenam eodem quo peccavit die Adamus luisset, nisi visum fuisset Deo ob futuram Christi Satisfactionem, spatium dare generi humano ad agendam poenitentiam, inquit Vir Doctus Disput. de lapsu Adami Thes. ultima. Denique aeternam omnino non incurrit, quia erat inter electos Dei, in quos infernus nihil habet juris. Apocal.
